## Declarations and implementations

```plato
//==
// # Joints
//
// Impulse bodies for the constraint types in `joints.types.plato`. A joint is
// solved exactly like a contact — an effective mass along a direction, a target
// relative speed, an impulse that is the difference divided by the mass — and the
// two share the kernels in `rigid-dynamics.library.plato` (`DirectionalMass`,
// `SeparationSpeed`, `ApplyImpulse`) rather than restating them.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Anchors
//  - Distance and rope constraints
//  - Ball-and-socket constraints
//  - Springs
//  - Solving a set of joints
//
// WHAT IS HERE AND WHAT IS NOT. The two joints this file solves are the two whose
// constraint is purely POSITIONAL: a distance joint holds one scalar and a
// ball-and-socket holds three. The hinge, the slider, the fixed joint and the
// six-degree-of-freedom joint all additionally constrain ORIENTATION, which needs
// an angular error measured as a quaternion difference and an angular effective
// mass that is the inverse-inertia sum rather than a scalar. That is a coherent
// second piece of work and is deliberately not begun here; `RevoluteJoint2D`,
// `HingeJoint`, `SliderJoint`, `FixedJoint`, `GenericJoint`, `PulleyJoint`,
// `GearConstraint` and the whole limit-and-motor apparatus (`AngularLimit`,
// `LinearLimit`, `JointMotor`, `JointBreakThreshold`) are declared and unsolved.
//
// TWO CONVENTIONS GOVERN EVERY BODY HERE:
//
//   * AN ANCHOR IS IN ITS OWN BODY'S LOCAL FRAME, as `joints.types.plato` states,
//     and is taken relative to that body's CENTRE OF MASS. The two coincide for
//     every primitive `MassPropertiesOf` produces, which puts the centre of mass
//     at the local origin; a body whose centre of mass is offset from its origin
//     must have its anchors given in centre-of-mass coordinates.
//   * BODY INDICES MUST BE VALID AND DISTINCT. The static world is an ordinary
//     body with zero inverse mass, not the index -1 — the same rule the contact
//     solver follows, and for the same reason: it removes every case analysis
//     from the solve.
//
// Joints here are solved WITHOUT accumulation across iterations: each visit
// computes the impulse the current velocities call for and applies it. Contacts
// accumulate because their impulse is one-sided and must be clamped against a
// running total; an equality constraint has no clamp, so its increments simply
// sum and the accumulator would be bookkeeping with no consequence. The two
// one-sided cases below — a rope at its limit, a distance joint at its minimum —
// clamp their increment's SIGN, which is the correct one-sided treatment for a
// constraint that is either active or absent rather than saturating.

library Joints
{
    //==
    // # Anchors

    // The world position of an anchor given in a body's local frame, relative to
    // its centre of mass.
    WorldAnchor(body: SolverBody3D, local: Point3D): Point3D
        => body.Center + local.Offset.Transform(body.Orientation);

    // The correction speed a positional error asks for: the error spread over one
    // step and scaled down, so the joint pulls itself together over several frames
    // instead of snapping. Zero stiffness leaves the joint purely a velocity
    // constraint, which drifts.
    JointBias(error: Number, stiffness: Number, seconds: Number): Number
        => -error * stiffness / seconds;

    //==
    // # Distance and rope constraints
    //
    // A distance joint holds the separation of its two anchors inside
    // [MinLength, MaxLength]. Equal bounds make a rigid rod, a zero minimum makes a
    // rope, and anything between is a rod with slack. Inside the range the joint
    // does nothing at all — that is what makes it a rope rather than a spring, and
    // it is why the constraint is solved only when it is violated.

    // How far the current separation lies outside the joint's allowed range:
    // positive when the anchors are too far apart, negative when they are too
    // close, and zero inside the range.
    DistanceError(joint: DistanceJoint, separation: Number): Number
        => separation > joint.MaxLength.Amount
            ? separation - joint.MaxLength.Amount
            : (separation < joint.MinLength.Amount ? separation - joint.MinLength.Amount : 0.0);

    // The two bodies after one visit to a distance joint. `stiffness` is the
    // fraction of the length error removed per step, in [0, 1].
    //
    // The impulse's sign is clamped to match the violation: a joint that is too
    // long may only pull and a joint that is too short may only push. Without that
    // clamp a rope would hold its ends apart as well as together, which is a rod.
    SolveJoint(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, joint: DistanceJoint, stiffness: Number,
        seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
    {
        var a = bodies[joint.BodyA.Value];
        var b = bodies[joint.BodyB.Value];
        var anchorA = WorldAnchor(a, joint.AnchorA);
        var anchorB = WorldAnchor(b, joint.AnchorB);
        var span = anchorA.Between(anchorB);
        var separation = span.Magnitude;
        var axis = separation > 0.0 ? span / separation : Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
        var error = DistanceError(joint, separation);
        var raw = ImpulseFor(
            JointBias(error, stiffness, seconds),
            SeparationSpeed(a, b, anchorA, anchorB, axis),
            DirectionalMass(a, b, anchorA, anchorB, axis));
        // Too long: pull, so the impulse on B must run back along -axis, i.e. be
        // negative. Too short: push, so it must be positive.
        var impulse = separation <= 0.0 || error == 0.0
            ? 0.0
            : (error > 0.0 ? raw.Min(0.0) : raw.Max(0.0));
        return ReplacedAt(
            ReplacedAt(bodies, joint.BodyA.Value, ApplyImpulse(a, axis * -impulse, anchorA)),
            joint.BodyB.Value,
            ApplyImpulse(b, axis * impulse, anchorB));
    }

    //==
    // # Ball-and-socket constraints
    //
    // A ball-and-socket holds its two anchors together and leaves orientation free:
    // three scalar equality constraints, one per world axis.
    //
    // They are solved ONE AXIS AT A TIME rather than as a coupled 3x3 block. The
    // block solve needs the inverse of the constraint's 3x3 effective-mass matrix
    // and converges in a single visit; the axis-at-a-time solve is Gauss-Seidel
    // over the three rows, needs no matrix inverse at all, and converges over the
    // iterations the solver is already running. The trade was taken because a 3x3
    // symmetric inverse is a piece of foundation vocabulary that does not yet
    // exist, and adding one to serve a single call site is the wrong shape of
    // dependency. It costs iterations, not correctness: the fixed point of the
    // three rows is the same point the block solve jumps to.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Seidel_method)

    // The two bodies after one visit to one axis of a ball-and-socket: drive the
    // relative anchor velocity along `axis` to the speed that closes the anchor
    // gap's component on that axis.
    SolveBallSocketAxis(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, joint: BallSocketJoint, axis: Vector3D,
        stiffness: Number, seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
    {
        var a = bodies[joint.BodyA.Value];
        var b = bodies[joint.BodyB.Value];
        var anchorA = WorldAnchor(a, joint.AnchorA);
        var anchorB = WorldAnchor(b, joint.AnchorB);
        var impulse = ImpulseFor(
            JointBias(anchorA.Between(anchorB).Dot(axis), stiffness, seconds),
            SeparationSpeed(a, b, anchorA, anchorB, axis),
            DirectionalMass(a, b, anchorA, anchorB, axis));
        return ReplacedAt(
            ReplacedAt(bodies, joint.BodyA.Value, ApplyImpulse(a, axis * -impulse, anchorA)),
            joint.BodyB.Value,
            ApplyImpulse(b, axis * impulse, anchorB));
    }
```
